'''''Quercus faginea''''', the '''Portuguese oak''', is a species of [[oak]] native to the western [[Mediterranean region]] in the [[Iberian Peninsula]]. Similar trees in the [[Atlas Mountains]] of northwest [[Africa]] are usually included in this species, or sometimes treated as a distinct species, ''Quercus tlemcenensis''. It occurs in mountains from sea level to {{Convert|1900|m|abbr=off}} above sea level, and flourishes in a variety of soils and climates. Out of all the [[Forests of the Iberian Peninsula|oak forests in the Iberian Peninsula]], the southern populations of Portuguese oak were found to have the highest diversity and [[endemism]] of spider species.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Malumbres-Olarte |first1=Jagoba |last2=Crespo |first2=Luís Carlos |last3=Domènech |first3=Marc |last4=Cardoso |first4=Pedro |last5=Moya-Laraño |first5=Jordi |last6=Ribera |first6=Carles |last7=Arnedo |first7=Miquel A. |title=How Iberian are we? Mediterranean climate determines structure and endemicity of spider communities in Iberian oak forests |journal=Biodiversity and Conservation |date=2020-12-01 |volume=29 |issue=14 |pages=3973–3996 |doi=10.1007/s10531-020-02058-7 |bibcode=2020BiCon..29.3973M |hdl=10138/337709 |s2cid=225151221 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10531-020-02058-7 |access-date=11 June 2021 |language=en |issn=1572-9710|hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Sequeira |first1=Inês |title=Cientistas descobrem que é nos bosques de carvalho-português que há mais espécies de aranhas |url=https://www.wilder.pt/historias/cientistas-descobrem-que-e-nos-bosques-de-carvalho-portugues-que-ha-mais-especies-de-aranhas/ |website=Wilder |access-date=11 June 2021 |language=pt-PT |date=2020-11-16}}</ref>

==Description==
''Q. faginea'' is a medium-sized [[deciduous]] or [[semi-evergreen]] [[tree]] growing to {{Convert|20|m|abbr=off}} tall, with a trunk up to {{Convert|80|cm|abbr=off}} in diameter, with grey-brown [[Bark (botany)|bark]]. The tree can live as long as 600 years. The [[leaves]] are {{Convert|4–10|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and 1.2–4 cm broad (rarely to 15 cm long and 5 cm broad), glossy dark green to gray-green above, and variably [[felted]] grey-white below; the margins have five to 12 pairs of irregular teeth. Leaf fall is typically in mid- to late winter. The [[flower]]s are [[catkin]]s, produced between March and April, almost always before [[Quercus rotundifolia|holm oak]], which grows in similar areas. The [[acorn]]s are oblong-ovoid, 2–2.5 cm long, maturing in 6 months to disperse in September or October.<ref>{{Flora Europaea |genus=Quercus |species=faginea}}</ref><ref>Bean, W. J. (1976). ''Trees and shrubs hardy in the British Isles'' 8th ed., revised. John Murray.</ref><ref>Rushforth, K. (1999). ''Trees of Britain and Europe''. HarperCollins {{ISBN|0-00-220013-9}}.</ref>

The species commonly develops [[gall]]s due to [[gall wasp]] activity; the galls are brown, 1–2 cm diameter, and have a spongy, cork-like interior.<ref>CAB International (2005). [http://www.cabicompendium.org/NamesLists/FC/Full/QUE_F1.htm data on ''Quercus faginea'', Forestry Compendium] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071009072143/http://www.cabicompendium.org/NamesLists/FC/Full/QUE_F1.htm |date=October 9, 2007 }}. Retrieved 27 July 2006.</ref>

Portuguese oak also [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridises]] readily with other related oaks such as [[Algerian oak]] (''Q. canariensis'') and [[downy oak]] (''Q. pubescens''), which can make identification difficult.{{citation needed|date=May 2026}}

The [[species|specific]] name ''faginea'' refers to the superficial resemblance of the leaves to those of the [[beech]] (''Fagus'').{{citation needed|date=May 2026}}

==Uses==
The [[wood]] has been used traditionally as firewood and as timber for construction (beams and posts). The acorns, like those of the [[quercus rotundifolia|holm oak]] or [[cork oak]], are an important food for free-range [[black Iberian pig]]s reared for ''[[jamón ibérico]]'' production. It is also occasionally planted as an [[ornamental tree]].{{citation needed|date=May 2026}}
